Today FS-02 receives only a full backup, which is a complete copy of all its data, once per night at 01:00. The infection began at 10:00. State whether the current backup schedule meets the RPO, roughly how much data could be lost, and suggest one change to the backup approach that would meet the 1-hour RPO.
subParts: Sequence the response using NIST phases
Order of volatility and chain of custody
modelAnswer: The correct order is c, d, e, a, b. First comes (c), confirming the alert with SIEM and EDR evidence and scoping the affected systems, which is Detection and Analysis. Next is (d), disconnecting FS-02 from the network, which is Containment. Then (e), deleting the malware and resetting the compromised account passwords, which is Eradication. After that, (a), restoring files from backup and returning the server to service, which is Recovery. Last is (b), the lessons-learned report and procedure updates, which is Post-Incident Activity. Preparation happened before the incident, so none of these five actions belongs to it. A strong answer notes that containment comes before eradication and recovery. If you restore files before the ransomware is contained and removed, the restored files can be encrypted again, and the infection may spread to other servers in the meantime.

Collect in this order: RAM contents first, then the running processes and active network connections, then files on the hard disk, and archived backup tapes last. RAM is erased the moment power is lost. Processes and connections change or end within seconds or minutes. Disk files survive a shutdown. Archived tapes are the most stable source. Note that some guides list processes and connections before or together with RAM, because a running process lives in memory. An answer that groups these two as the most volatile, before the disk and tapes, should be accepted. A chain of custody record is a written log of who collected each piece of evidence, when and where they collected it, and every person who handled or transferred it afterwards. It matters because it proves the evidence was not altered or tampered with. Without it, the evidence may be rejected in legal or disciplinary action. Shutting FS-02 down before capturing RAM would permanently destroy that evidence, so the collection order has real consequences.

Fix Finding B first, the CVSS 8.1 weakness on the internet-facing VPN gateway. It is directly reachable by attackers on the internet, and threat intelligence shows it is being actively exploited right now, so the real risk of compromise is highest there. A CVSS score measures how severe a weakness is in general. It does not tell you how exposed your particular system is or whether attackers are currently using the weakness. Finding A has the highest score, 9.8, but the test server is not connected to the company network or the internet, so it is very hard for an attacker to reach. It can be scheduled after B. Finding C is moderate and reachable only internally, so it comes last. Prioritizing by score alone would leave the gateway open to an active, ongoing threat.

No, the current schedule does not meet the 1-hour RPO. The last good backup was taken at 01:00 and the infection began at 10:00, so about 9 hours of changes could be lost. In the worst case, with a failure just before the next nightly backup, nearly 24 hours could be lost. Any change that captures data at least once per hour meets the RPO. One good answer is to keep the nightly full backup and add hourly incremental backups. An incremental backup copies only the data that changed since the last backup of any kind. Another good answer is hourly differential backups, which copy everything changed since the last full backup. Hourly snapshots or replication would also work. A strong answer also notes that backups should be kept offline or protected so the ransomware cannot encrypt them. It also notes that restoring must be tested to fit within the 4-hour RTO, because meeting the RPO alone does not guarantee the server is back in time.

scenarios.title: Copperleaf Outfitters: Risk Math, Policy Paperwork, and a New Vendor
scenarios.scenario:
You have just joined Copperleaf Outfitters, a fictional online shop that sells camping gear. It is based in the United States, takes credit card payments on its website, and has many customers living in the European Union (EU). Your manager, Dana, is preparing a short report for the leadership team and has given you four tasks.

First, some background on the risk numbers. The customer order database has an asset value (AV), meaning what it would cost the business to replace or recover it, of $200,000. The team estimates that one ransomware attack, which is malware that locks files until a payment is made, would damage 25% of that value. That percentage is called the exposure factor (EF). History suggests such an attack happens about once every two years, so the annualized rate of occurrence (ARO), meaning the expected number of times per year, is 0.5. The single loss expectancy (SLE) is the cost of one incident, calculated as AV x EF. The annualized loss expectancy (ALE) is the expected loss per year, calculated as SLE x ARO. A vendor offers an endpoint protection service, which is software that watches each computer for malicious behaviour. It costs $18,000 per year and is expected to cut the ARO from 0.5 to 0.1.

Second, Dana found four documents in a shared folder and is not sure how to label them. Document A says: "All company and customer data must be protected from unauthorized access." Document B says: "Passwords must be at least 14 characters long." Document C says: "To reset a user's multifactor authentication token, open the admin console, select the user, click Reset, then confirm the user's identity by phone." Multifactor authentication means logging in with more than one kind of proof, such as a password plus a phone code. Document D says: "Staff are encouraged to use a password manager." A password manager is an app that stores and generates passwords.

Third, Copperleaf is signing a contract with CloudVault, a company that will store nightly backup copies of the order database. CloudVault is a third party, meaning an outside organisation that handles Copperleaf's data. Leadership wants a written right in the contract that lets Copperleaf, or an auditor it hires, inspect CloudVault's security controls. An auditor is an independent reviewer who checks whether rules are being followed.

Fourth, leadership asks which outside rules apply to Copperleaf. The candidates are GDPR (the EU General Data Protection Regulation, a law protecting the personal data of people in the EU), HIPAA (the US Health Insurance Portability and Accountability Act, a law protecting patient health information), and PCI DSS (the Payment Card Industry Data Security Standard, a set of security requirements created by the major card brands for any business that stores, processes, or sends card data).

1. Calculate the SLE and the current ALE for ransomware against the order database. Then calculate the new ALE with the endpoint protection service, and state whether the $18,000 yearly cost is justified by the numbers.
2. Label Documents A, B, C, and D as a policy, standard, procedure, or guideline, and explain which ones staff must follow.
3. Name the contract clause leadership wants with CloudVault and explain why it matters for third-party risk.
4. State which of GDPR, HIPAA, and PCI DSS apply to Copperleaf and give the reason for each, including any that do not apply.
subParts: Risk math: SLE, ALE, and control cost
modelAnswer: SLE = AV x EF = $200,000 x 0.25 = $50,000 per incident. Current ALE = SLE x ARO = $50,000 x 0.5 = $25,000 per year. With the control, the new ALE = $50,000 x 0.1 = $5,000 per year. The yearly loss reduction is $25,000 - $5,000 = $20,000. That is more than the $18,000 yearly cost, so the control is justified, with a net benefit of $2,000 per year. Full credit requires the correct figures and the comparison of the $20,000 reduction against the $18,000 cost. A common mistake is to compare the $18,000 cost to the new ALE of $5,000, or to multiply AV by ARO and skip the exposure factor.

Document A is a policy: a broad, high-level statement of what management requires and why, with no technical detail. Document B is a standard: a specific, measurable rule that supports the policy. Document C is a procedure: step-by-step instructions for carrying out a task. Document D is a guideline: a recommendation that is encouraged but optional. Policies, standards, and procedures are mandatory for staff. Guidelines are not mandatory. A common mistake is to treat the password manager advice as a requirement, or to call the 14-character rule a policy. The hierarchy runs from general, mandatory policy down to detailed standards and procedures, with guidelines as optional advice.

The clause is a right-to-audit clause. It gives Copperleaf, or an auditor it hires, the contractual right to inspect CloudVault's security controls. This matters because Copperleaf's customer data will sit with an outside company Copperleaf does not control. Copperleaf still carries the risk and the compliance responsibility if CloudVault is breached. The clause lets Copperleaf check the vendor's security instead of simply trusting its claims. Without it, Copperleaf may have no way to confirm that its backups are protected. Answers that name only a service level agreement (uptime or performance promises) do not meet the requirement, because that kind of agreement does not grant inspection rights.

PCI DSS applies because Copperleaf takes credit card payments on its website. It is an industry standard enforced through contracts with the card brands, not a government law. GDPR applies because Copperleaf handles the personal data of customers living in the EU, even though the company is based in the United States. HIPAA does not apply because Copperleaf is a retailer and does not handle patient health information. Full credit requires all three judgements with reasons. A common mistake is to assume GDPR covers only companies located in the EU, when it follows the EU residents' data wherever the business is based.
